name: Team MRG
subject: Final Week for Signatures
body:
Hi Volunteers,
Thank you for all your support to get signatures for Mark Robert Gordon.
He is filing on Friday March 20th. We will be pushing to get as many
signatures as possible this week and can do a canvass this weekend and file
supplemental signatures on Monday March 23td.
If you can help with the final push, please fill out this google form.
https://forms.gle/Fh7whFYs33d8Tubu7

If you are making calls or helping with data, thank you as well and please
reach out if you need more calling lists or data.

If you have petition pages to turn in, please let me know so I can arrange
to pick them up. I will be reaching out directly via text or phone as
well, so please make sure you are not filtering or blocking unknown numbers
or add me to your contacts..

Best Regards,
Mary Fortney
(602) 376-7453

People usually phrase it as having "fuck you money." The idea that you have enough freedom and security that you can say exactly what you want, do what you want, and be completely yourself without worrying about the consequences.
If you have that kind of freedom, the consequences of what you say do not really affect your livelihood, your social circle, your family, or your position in the world. You live outside many of the boundaries that other people have to live within.
And that idea made me start thinking about the word authenticity.
And because I live in the political space, and because I am The Angry Democrat, I want to talk about what authenticity actually means when we talk about political candidates.
## My Own Struggle With Authenticity
I have been interviewing candidates recently, and I have also been a candidate myself twice.
One of the most common pieces of advice you hear in politics is simple.
"Just be authentic."
But I remember my 2022 campaign clearly. I was the furthest thing from authentic.
I was trying to craft a message that I thought would resonate with everybody. I did not want to come down too hard on certain issues because I did not want to alienate voters. I also did not want to make people mad who I might need as allies. You know, the, "reach across the aisle! Compromise!" approach.
So my authentic self was not really present.
Sure, people thought I was a nice guy. Some people liked me more than my opponent. Obviously not everybody, because I lost.
But I still had supporters.
But, the question I wrestled with was whether I was actually being authentic.
And if I was not, why not?
## The Boundaries Around Authenticity
I give people the advice all the time. Just be yourself. Be authentic.
But to truly be yourself, you have to live without certain boundaries.
Even people who appear authentic are still operating within some kind of structure. Someone may say whatever they want, act however they want, and appear to live freely. But in politics that can be just as much of a gimmick as someone who carefully guards their opinions.
Sometimes authenticity itself becomes a strategy.
But the truth is that most people have something to lose.
When someone believes they have something to lose, and when the loss feels more important than the potential gain, authenticity takes a back seat.
Even when you think you are being authentic, there is always a moment where you pause and ask yourself questions.
Do I really believe this?
Do I really want to say this?
Am I willing to make this person mad?
Am I willing to make this group mad?
Am I willing to lose a friend or a family member?

## The Lines We Choose Not to Cross
Some decisions are easy. Sometimes you know it is time to cut the rope with someone in your life.
But most situations are not that clear.
Sometimes the question becomes what are you actually sacrificing?
I have a couple of friends where there are certain political topics we simply do not talk about. And, these are people I talk about politics with all the time.
But for the sake of our friendship, we either had conversations about boundaries or we have an unspoken agreement not to go there.
We know there are strong beliefs on both sides.
So some topics are simply better left unsaid.
Does that make me inauthentic? Do I guard myself on those topics because of friendships?
It is something I have been wrestling with.
What is there to gain by being completely authentic?
And what is there to lose?
## Authenticity Fears
One of the biggest fears about authenticity is the possibility that your authenticity turns out to be ignorance.
Maybe you stand firmly on something and later realize you were wrong.
Maybe you change your opinion later.
That ignorance or misinformation destroys a friendship or burns a bridge that cannot be repaired.
And maybe you later find yourself holding the exact opposite view or that the facts around the view you held were wrong.
Those are the risks people quietly think about when they decide whether to speak their mind. When you take a hard stand on something, you are putting your identity behind it. You are telling people this is what you believe and this is who you are.
But people grow. People learn. Circumstances change.
And sometimes the thing you were absolutely certain about turns out to be incomplete, misunderstood, or flat out wrong.
If that authenticity cost you relationships along the way, the damage may already be done. A friendship may already be broken. A bridge may already be burned. A person you once respected may no longer be part of your life.
That possibility alone makes people cautious.
Because authenticity does not just carry the risk of being criticized in the moment. It carries the risk that someday you might look back and realize the person you were so certain about being was not the person you are anymore.

## Authenticity Is a Privilege
I believe authenticity is a privilege.
It is something available to people whose world revolves around themselves in a way that cannot easily break. No matter what happens, their world remains intact because they are the center of it. Their decisions, their opinions, and their voice do not depend as heavily on keeping everyone around them satisfied.
Authenticity also belongs to people who have reached a realization about themselves and their place in the world. They understand that if everything around them were to fall apart because of something they said or believed, they could still live with that outcome.
They understand the consequences and accept them.
At the end of the day, they know they will still be standing.
Friends or no friends.
Family or no family.
They understand that their life ultimately belongs to them, and that realization creates a kind of freedom. It allows them to say what they believe, even when they know it might upset people or create conflict.
That realization, that willingness to accept the consequences of being fully yourself, is what makes authenticity possible. And that is why authenticity is not just a personality trait. It not just a choice. It is not a way of acting during a campaign.
It is a privilege.
## The Evolution of a Candidate
As a candidate trying to find your authentic voice is hard.
It means pushing against the fear that people will be mad at you.
It means pushing against the fear that people will say your opinions are worthless or invalid.
It means figuring out what you actually believe and which things deserve a strong voice.
At the same time, it is asking does everything deserve a voice?
Authenticity is not about shouting every thought you have. It is about being thoughtful, confident, assertive, and mindful.
And it means understanding that some people will not like you. And that is ok.
Some people will not like what you say. And that is ok.
Some people will not like what you stand for. And that is ok.
Every political candidate experiences this process.
#### At least the good ones do.
There is a cycle I have noticed.
At first, candidates are terrified. Myself included.
They write speeches. They stand in front of people. Their voices crack. Their hands shake. They are nervous as hell trying to get through a stump speech they have practiced a hundred times.
They do not want to disappoint people.
They do not want to get laughed at.
They do not want to say the wrong thing.
Eventually they get more comfortable. They learn how to deliver the speech better.
But the speech itself usually does not change.
The candidates I watch most closely are the ones who eventually challenge themselves.
The ones who get angry at the system.
The ones who notice when the media plays favorites.
When the party plays favorites.
When the thumb is clearly on the scale.
At that point, candidates face a choice.
Some decide they **just need to play the game better so that the system favors them next time.**
Others cannot ignore the injustice. It bothers them too much.
Those are the candidates I pay attention to. The candidates who find their voice. The ones who refuse to accept the unfairness.
They begin their campaigns trying to please everyone. They try to get every vote possible for an abstract idea of winning.
But over time they evolve.
They begin speaking their truth.
They start raising ideas that may be unpopular but address real problems people see coming.
They begin advocating for solutions they genuinely believe in, even when those ideas are outside the normal political playbook.
They start speaking honestly about how systems might need to change.
And through that authentic voice they begin to build real alliances, real coalitions, and real change.
But even that process is a privilege.
The ability to speak up is a privilege.
The ability to have strong opinions publicly is a privilege.
The ability to lose a friend, a colleague, a job, a family member, or political party loyalty because of political disagreement is a privilege.
And the ability to not fear those consequences is privilege.

## The Hard Road to Authenticity
I describe this moment as a realization.
The realization that you have to live your own life.
And that if you do that, the people who truly belong in your life will remain.
But not everyone reaches that point.
The journey is difficult.
For some people it never gets completed.
Sometimes people lose more than they gain. They live with regret.
For many people, inauthenticity becomes the only way to survive.
And that is **not** something I say with judgment.
When I say authenticity is a privilege, I mean that very literally.
## A Question Worth Asking
Through my experience running for office twice, interviewing candidates for podcasts, working with the party, and now writing as The Angry Democrat, I have seen many different types of candidates.
I have also seen my own evolution.
So I encourage people to ask themselves a question. Even if you are not a political candidate.
What do you do?
Do you walk away and try to figure out how to play the game better so the system eventually favors you? Or do you challenge yourself?
Do you develop clear ideas, clear values, and move forward knowing that authenticity may come with consequences?
Because authenticity always comes with an uncertain future.
And the decision to act on it is always a privilege.

"Just do the right thing. The rest doesn't matter." \- **Marcus Aurelius**

Please consider sharing and subscribing to fuel the ANGER for change. The quiet calculation behind every opinion a candidate shares | | | Mar 16 | | | | | | | | | | | | This article might be a little bit of what people now call "slop." A little bit all over the place. But it is something I have been thinking about recently, even though the idea itself is actually very old. | | ---|---|--- People usually phrase it as having "fuck you money." The idea that you have enough freedom and security that you can say exactly what you want, do what you want, and be completely yourself without worrying about the consequences. If you have that kind of freedom, the consequences of what you say do not really affect your livelihood, your social circle, your family, or your position in the world. You live outside many of the boundaries that other people have to live within. And that idea made me start thinking about the word authenticity. And because I live in the political space, and because I am The Angry Democrat, I want to talk about what authenticity actually means when we talk about political candidates. My Own Struggle With Authenticity I have been interviewing candidates recently, and I have also been a candidate myself twice. One of the most common pieces of advice you hear in politics is simple. "Just be authentic." But I remember my 2022 campaign clearly. I was the furthest thing from authentic. I was trying to craft a message that I thought would resonate with everybody. I did not want to come down too hard on certain issues because I did not want to alienate voters. I also did not want to make people mad who I might need as allies. You know, the, "reach across the aisle! Compromise!" approach. So my authentic self was not really present. Sure, people thought I was a nice guy. Some people liked me more than my opponent. Obviously not everybody, because I lost. But I still had supporters. But, the question I wrestled with was whether I was actually being authentic. And if I was not, why not? The Boundaries Around Authenticity I give people the advice all the time. Just be yourself. Be authentic. But to truly be yourself, you have to live without certain boundaries. Even people who appear authentic are still operating within some kind of structure. Someone may say whatever they want, act however they want, and appear to live freely. But in politics that can be just as much of a gimmick as someone who carefully guards their opinions. Sometimes authenticity itself becomes a strategy. But the truth is that most people have something to lose. When someone believes they have something to lose, and when the loss feels more important than the potential gain, authenticity takes a back seat. Even when you think you are being authentic, there is always a moment where you pause and ask yourself questions. Do I really believe this? Do I really want to say this? Am I willing to make this person mad? Am I willing to make this group mad? Am I willing to lose a friend or a family member? ? The Lines We Choose Not to Cross Some decisions are easy. Sometimes you know it is time to cut the rope with someone in your life. But most situations are not that clear. Sometimes the question becomes what are you actually sacrificing? I have a couple of friends where there are certain political topics we simply do not talk about. And, these are people I talk about politics with all the time. But for the sake of our friendship, we either had conversations about boundaries or we have an unspoken agreement not to go there. We know there are strong beliefs on both sides. So some topics are simply better left unsaid. Does that make me inauthentic? Do I guard myself on those topics because of friendships? It is something I have been wrestling with. What is there to gain by being completely authentic? And what is there to lose? Authenticity Fears One of the biggest fears about authenticity is the possibility that your authenticity turns out to be ignorance. Maybe you stand firmly on something and later realize you were wrong. Maybe you change your opinion later. That ignorance or misinformation destroys a friendship or burns a bridge that cannot be repaired. And maybe you later find yourself holding the exact opposite view or that the facts around the view you held were wrong. Those are the risks people quietly think about when they decide whether to speak their mind. When you take a hard stand on something, you are putting your identity behind it. You are telling people this is what you believe and this is who you are. But people grow. People learn. Circumstances change. And sometimes the thing you were absolutely certain about turns out to be incomplete, misunderstood, or flat out wrong. If that authenticity cost you relationships along the way, the damage may already be done. A friendship may already be broken. A bridge may already be burned. A person you once respected may no longer be part of your life. That possibility alone makes people cautious. Because authenticity does not just carry the risk of being criticized in the moment. It carries the risk that someday you might look back and realize the person you were so certain about being was not the person you are anymore. Authenticity Is a Privilege I believe authenticity is a privilege. It is something available to people whose world revolves around themselves in a way that cannot easily break. No matter what happens, their world remains intact because they are the center of it. Their decisions, their opinions, and their voice do not depend as heavily on keeping everyone around them satisfied. Authenticity also belongs to people who have reached a realization about themselves and their place in the world. They understand that if everything around them were to fall apart because of something they said or believed, they could still live with that outcome. They understand the consequences and accept them. At the end of the day, they know they will still be standing. Friends or no friends. Family or no family. They understand that their life ultimately belongs to them, and that realization creates a kind of freedom. It allows them to say what they believe, even when they know it might upset people or create conflict. That realization, that willingness to accept the consequences of being fully yourself, is what makes authenticity possible. And that is why authenticity is not just a personality trait. It not just a choice. It is not a way of acting during a campaign. It is a privilege. The Evolution of a Candidate As a candidate trying to find your authentic voice is hard. It means pushing against the fear that people will be mad at you. It means pushing against the fear that people will say your opinions are worthless or invalid. It means figuring out what you actually believe and which things deserve a strong voice. At the same time, it is asking does everything deserve a voice? Authenticity is not about shouting every thought you have. It is about being thoughtful, confident, assertive, and mindful. And it means understanding that some people will not like you. And that is ok. Some people will not like what you say. And that is ok. Some people will not like what you stand for. And that is ok. Every political candidate experiences this process. At least the good ones do. There is a cycle I have noticed. At first, candidates are terrified. Myself included. They write speeches. They stand in front of people. Their voices crack. Their hands shake. They are nervous as hell trying to get through a stump speech they have practiced a hundred times. They do not want to disappoint people. They do not want to get laughed at. They do not want to say the wrong thing. Eventually they get more comfortable. They learn how to deliver the speech better. But the speech itself usually does not change. The candidates I watch most closely are the ones who eventually challenge themselves. The ones who get angry at the system. The ones who notice when the media plays favorites. When the party plays favorites. When the thumb is clearly on the scale. At that point, candidates face a choice. Some decide they just need to play the game better so that the system favors them next time. Others cannot ignore the injustice. It bothers them too much. Those are the candidates I pay attention to. The candidates who find their voice. The ones who refuse to accept the unfairness. They begin their campaigns trying to please everyone. They try to get every vote possible for an abstract idea of winning. But over time they evolve. They begin speaking their truth. They start raising ideas that may be unpopular but address real problems people see coming. They begin advocating for solutions they genuinely believe in, even when those ideas are outside the normal political playbook. They start speaking honestly about how systems might need to change. And through that authentic voice they begin to build real alliances, real coalitions, and real change. But even that process is a privilege. The ability to speak up is a privilege. The ability to have strong opinions publicly is a privilege. The ability to lose a friend, a colleague, a job, a family member, or political party loyalty because of political disagreement is a privilege. And the ability to not fear those consequences is privilege. ? The Hard Road to Authenticity I describe this moment as a realization. The realization that you have to live your own life. And that if you do that, the people who truly belong in your life will remain. But not everyone reaches that point. The journey is difficult. For some people it never gets completed. Sometimes people lose more than they gain. They live with regret. For many people, inauthenticity becomes the only way to survive. And that is not something I say with judgment. When I say authenticity is a privilege, I mean that very literally. A Question Worth Asking Through my experience running for office twice, interviewing candidates for podcasts, working with the party, and now writing as The Angry Democrat, I have seen many different types of candidates. I have also seen my own evolution. So I encourage people to ask themselves a question. Even if you are not a political candidate. What do you do? Do you walk away and try to figure out how to play the game better so the system eventually favors you? Or do you challenge yourself? Do you develop clear ideas, clear values, and move forward knowing that authenticity may come with consequences? Because authenticity always comes with an uncertain future. And the decision to act on it is always a privilege. "Just do the right thing. The rest doesn't matter." \- Marcus Aurelius Stay Angry. Join otherANGRY DEMOCRATS** by support Matt's work. body:
As Trump pulls the U.S. deeper into another unstable and dangerous Middle East quagmire, his dark agenda to dismantle free and fair elections at home is at risk.
| | | | | [](https://6s79z9hbb.cc.rs6.net/tn.jsp?f=001ZYmHNpEENm_XunKK_b4kPTx2-OHaGntFwZhNvL9O-iDZ6SbBSqFsGXSx7JS50B2PSwQoI0livoe2ry4thQPOIUZU_esI_GvgZX_zWz1PurW5qTeaNZl7QzaX8bCUK3KEWZQUbw7iHGDSH83Ippj2uUmJp_9NKfR4cUKDEk2dgNPIDFw_HM6hN8n8_kXUufv3B42IMaa0At95IxcH8WOudlr6ZZyphxAG&c=yGlgttRI8GvG29BXlENEDravnlQttVDk8Cl_Fg-vTsz3WiHeJjpMXA==&ch=xXH2iMHfuTnlgB0Goc8fyP25YdxONZH90wRcO1JpeDwxekD-cPac8g==)
---
Peter,
Trump's historic unpopularity and international blunders are complicating MAGA's push to rig the midterm election.
In Florida, the GOP is rapidly descending into chaos as Republican leaders split on how they can gerrymander to net more red seats. Florida is getting hit hard by the fallout of the Iran war and Trump's massive cuts to health care.
The war in Iran has backfired. Gas prices are soaring. The cost for food and other everyday items is poised to skyrocket.
Iran's willingness to fight and to strangle oil exports and other commerce in the Strait of Hormuz caught Trump and his incompetent sycophants in charge of our national security off guard.
The effects of Trump's disastrous decision to attack Iran are being felt worldwide, and our economy looks headed for a recession.

_And I stopped it before._

**It started in 1998 when I was Speaker of the House.**

The Clinton Administration attempted to fundamentally corrupt the U.S. Census.

Their plan was called _" statistical sampling."_

**In plain English, it would have allowed unelected bureaucrats to manufacture population numbers instead of counting _real people, one at a time._**

Red states would be undercounted.
Blue states would be completely inflated.
Congressional seats would be rigged before a single vote was cast.

It was a direct assault on representative government, Peter.

_**So I sued Bill Clinton --and won.**_

The Supreme Court sided with me in a nail-biting 5-4 ruling.
They agreed the only legitimate way to count the Census was by a _strict, physical headcount._

That victory protected the integrity of our elections for a generation.

| | Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw

Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. | | **FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE****Date:** March 16, 2026 **Contact:**[**Taylor Gillespie**](mailto:taylorg@eileenforcolorado.com)**,** 720-557-6185
**Record Turnout: More Voters Backed Eileen Laubacher Than Attended the Last Two Assemblies Combined**
_Laubacher Wins Over 85% of Delegates Across District_
**Highlands Ranch** \- Over the last two weeks, hundreds of voters showed up across congressional district four to show their support for Eileen Laubacher. Eileen received nearly 900 of the 1200 votes cast across the state. In 2024 and 2022, there were less than a total of 800 people who turned out to vote for all the candidates. The record attendance was evident all across the district, and it is clear that voters are ready for Retired Rear Admiral Eileen Laubacher to take the fight to Lauren Boebert. Of the 168 delegates elected across the district, 143 delegates — more than 85 percent — were chosen by their peers to support Retired Rear Admiral Eileen Laubacher at the upcoming CD-4 assemb“The turnout across the district shows voters are energized and ready for change,” **said Retired Rear Admiral Eileen Laubacher.** “They have put their trust in this campaign because we’ve shown up, listened and done the hard work - that is exactly how I’ll serve in Congress and the fight that I will take to Lauren Boebert.”Support for Laubacher was strong and consistent across the entire district. In Douglas County—the district’s largest—delegates overwhelmingly backed Laubacher, winning all 92 delegates elected there, while rural counties across the district also delivered decisive support. In communities like Cheyenne, Kit Carson, and Logan counties, Laubacher won all of the delegates as turnout surged to historic levels. From small rural communities to the suburbs, voters showed up in record numbers and delivered overwhelming support for Laubacher, underscoring the broad coalition forming across the district to defeat Lauren Boebert in November.**Since launching, the campaign has:**
* Held **58 meet-and-greets** across the district with over 1,600 attendees.
* Engaged **over 900 first-time caucus-goers**
* Made **29,000 calls** to past and new caucus-goers
* Mobilized **over 100 veterans** who committed to caucus for Eileen
* Recruited **more than 900 volunteers**
* Helped **over 130 supporters switch their registration from UAF to DEM** to caucus for Eileen (a conservative estimate)
* Elected **482 brand-new caucus-goers as County Delegates** to support Eileen.

The energy behind Laubacher’s campaign reflects a true grassroots movement built through months of organizing across the district. Shortly after launching, Retired Rear Admiral Eileen Laubacher and her team began traveling across the district — visiting nearly every county, meeting with communities, and engaging directly with rural hospitals, veterans’ organizations, and local leaders. The campaign consistently urged voters that meeting this moment required more than support — it required showing up and getting involved.
That organizing paid off at caucus and county assemblies, where more than half of the voters supporting Laubacher were first-time caucus participants. More than 100 veterans also turned out in support after meeting Laubacher at community gatherings across the district. The historic turnout was no accident — it was the result of sustained grassroots engagement and a growing coalition of voters ready to defeat Lauren Boebert and elect a representative who will show up and deliver for Colorado.“As we look ahead to November, this election will be won by the candidate who puts in the work, listens to voters, and shows up consistently,”**Laubacher added**. “That’s what this campaign has done from day one, and we’re just getting started.”**For more information,** or to get involved in the campaign, visit [eileenforcolorado.com](https://eileenforcolorado.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=400e8fa21dba23169b817268c&id=aeb0097c9d&e=1c5f08419c).##

Lifе and death Son of Mykhailo Sulyma, Ivan came from a petty noble (szlachta) family. He was born in Rohoshchi (next to Chernihiv). He served as an estate overseer for Stanisław Żółkiewski and later the family of Daniłowicze who inherited his lands; for that service in 1620 he was awarded three villages: Sulimówka, Kuczakiw and Lebedyn. Аll the villages todаy belong to the Boryspil Raion, Kyiv Oblast. His sons included Stepan (died 1659), a captain of Boryspil company, and Fedir (died 1691), a colonel of Pereiaslav regiment. He became popular among the unregistered Cossacks, leading them on campaigns to plunder Crimea and other Ottoman vassal territories. For organizing a revolt on an Ottoman slave galley and freeing Christian slaves[1] he received a medal from Pope Paul V himself. Eventually, Sulyma reached the rank of the hetman, which he held from 1628 to 1629 and 1630 to 1635. In 1635, after returning from an expedition to Black Sea against the Ottomans, he decided to rebel against the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, which at that time controlled most of the Cossack territories, and whose nobility was trying to turn militant Cossacks into serfs.[citation needed] Ivan Sulyma took part in numerous campaigns of Sagaidachny against Tatars and Turks. In particular, it was the famous capture of Kafa (modern Theodosia), the main center of the slave trade on the Black Sea, Trapezont, Izmail, and also two attacks on Tsaregrad. On the night of 3 to 4 August 1635 he took the newly constructed Kodak fortress by surprise, burning it and executing its crew of about 200 people under Jean Marion. Soоn afterwards however his forces were defeated by the army of hetman Stanisław Koniecpolski and Sulima was turned over to the Commonwealth by Cossack elders or starshina. Together with several other leaders of his rebellion, Hetman Sulyma was executed in Warsaw on 12 December 1635. At first, the Polish King Władysław IV Waza, known for his friendly attitude towards the Cossacks, was hesitant to execute Sulyma, especially since he was a person upon whom the Pope himself bestowed his medal. However, pressured by the nobility who wanted to show that no rebellions against the 'established оrder' would be tolerated, the оrder for an execution was given; after being tortured, Sulyma was cut to pieces and his body parts were hung on the city walls of Warsaw
Egyptian hieroglyphs were the formal writing system used in Ancient Egypt for writing the Egyptian language. Hieroglyphs combined logographic, syllabic and alphabetic elements, with some 1,000 distinct characters.[3][4] Cursive hieroglyphs were used for religious literature on papyrus and wood. The later hieratic and demotic Egyptian scripts were derived from hieroglyphic writing, as was the Proto-Sinaitic script that later evolved into the Phoenician alphabet.[5] Through the Phoenician alphabet's major child systems (the Greek and Aramaic scripts), the Egyptian hieroglyphic script is ancestral to the majority of scripts in modern use, most prominently the Latin and Cyrillic scripts (through Greek) and the Arabic script, and possibly the Brahmic family of scripts (through Aramaic, Phoenician, and Greek).[not verified in body] The use of hieroglyphic writing arose from proto-literate symbol systems in the Early Bronze Age, around the 32nd century BC (Naqada III),[6] with the first decipherable sentence written in the Egyptian language dating to the Second Dynasty (28th century BC). Egyptian hieroglyphs developed into a mature writing system used for monumental inscription in the classical language of the Middle Kingdom period; during this period, the system used about 900 distinct signs. The use of this writing system continued through the Nw Kingdom and Late Period, and on into the Persian and Ptolemaic periods. Late survivals of hieroglyphic use are found well into the Roman period, extending into the 4th century AD.[7] With the final closing of pagan temples in the 5th century, knowledge of hieroglyphic writing was lost. Although attempts were made, the script remained undeciphered throughout the Middle Ages and the early modern period. The decipherment of hieroglyphic writing was finally accomplished in the 1820s by Jean-François Champollion, with the help of the Rosetta Stone.[8] The number of words contained in al Ancient Egyptian (i.e. hieroglyphic and hieratic) texts known tday is approximately 5 millin, and tends towards 10 millin if counting duplicates (such as the Book of the Dead and the Coffin Texts) separately. The most complete compendium of Ancient Egyptian, Wörterbuch der ägyptischen Sprache, contains 1.5–1.7 millin words.[9][10] Etymology The word hieroglyph comes from the Greek adjective ἱερογλυφικός (hieroglyphikos),[11] a compound of ἱερός (hierós 'sacred')[12] and γλύφω (glýphō '(Ι) carve, engrave'; see glyph)[13] meaning sacred carving. The glyphs themselves, since the Ptolemaic period, were called τὰ ἱερογλυφικὰ [γράμματα] (tà hieroglyphikà [grámmata]) "the sacred engraved letters", the Greek counterpart to the Egyptian expression of mdw.w-nṯr "god's words".[14] Greek ἱερόγλυφος meant "a carver of hieroglyphs".[15] In English, hieroglyph as a noun is recorded from 1590, originally short for nominalized hieroglyphic (1580s, with a plural hieroglyphics), from adjectival use (hieroglyphic character).[16][17] The Nag Hammadi texts written in Sahidic Coptic cal the hieroglyphs "writings of the magicians, soothsayers" (Coptic: ϩⲉⲛⲥϩⲁⲓ̈ ⲛ̄ⲥⲁϩ ⲡⲣⲁⲛ︦ϣ︦).[18]

Recently, the U.S. House of Representatives officially voted to pass the so-called SAVE America Act, which would result in the disenfranchisement of millions of eligible voters. body:
We already rejected MAGA talking points in New Hampshire. Now national Republicans are dusting off their playbook.
# [](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/126?t=1&akid=5603%2E582294%2Eo1lbIf)
**I’m sorry about Karoline Leavitt.**
A few years ago, Karoline Leavitt ran against me for Congress here in New Hampshire. Her campaign was steeped in extreme MAGA rhetoric and zero connection to the actual issues Granite Staters face every day. **Voters saw right through it and rejected her agenda by nearly 10 points.**
[](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260316_1.SdHT4P&refcode=em20260316-1&t=2&akid=5603%2E582294%2Eo1lbIf)
Unfortunately that race turned into a national audition. Now the same talking points and spin that New Hampshire voters dismissed are being used daily from the White House briefing room.
So if you’re wondering how the rest of the country ended up having to listen to Karoline Leavitt, it’s because New Hampshire proved something important first: Her extreme ideas don’t hold up when you put them in front of real voters.
But that hasn’t stopped the MAGA machine from trying. **National Republicans are pouring money into New Hampshire because they think they can break through and notch a win here to cling to their Senate majority.** They’ve lined up behind John Sununu, an NRSC-backed candidate who will vote with Donald Trump and MAGA leadership when it matters most. It’s a new candidate reading from the same old playbook.
I’ve beaten their playbook before by focusing on kitchen-table issues, standing up for families, and telling the truth. **[Now I need your help to do it again. Will you chip in $5 to help us keep this Senate seat blue and fight on what matters to Granite Staters?](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260316_1.SdHT4P&refcode=em20260316-1&t=3&akid=5603%2E582294%2Eo1lbIf)**
Granite Staters value independence. They reward common sense. And they don’t like being sold a script written somewhere else.
If you believe New Hampshire should keep leading the way and showing the rest of the country that MAGA politics don’t work here, I’m asking you to be a part of our campaign. **If Democrats are going to flip the Senate, we need to win this open race in New Hampshire.**
**[Will you chip in to help us keep this Senate seat blue and stop national Republicans from installing another vote for Trump’s agenda?](https://act.chrispappas.org/go/181?c0=em_ms_cp_20260316_1.SdHT4P&refcode=em20260316-1&t=4&akid=5603%2E582294%2Eo1lbIf)**

Thanks for being in this fight with me.
Chris

Slowly but surely, the outcry over Democrats' ridiculous stunt to keep certain parts of the Department of Homeland Security defunded, while ICE remains funded, is reaching a boiling point.
The most visible impact from the Democrats' powerplay are long lines for security at an increasing number of the country's airports. From Austin to Atlanta, wait times have risen up to four hours. subject: How I'll fight voter suppression
disclaimer_text: paid for by Joe Jaworski Campaign
body:
Requiring voters to produce birth certificates and documents to prove citizenship before they can register is a stunt designed to suppress the vote. | | | [View this email in your browser](https://mailchi.mp/jaworskifortexas.com/last-night-14193438?e=5d8d80652b)
---
| | [ ](https://jaworskifortexas.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2e1f50319ad85f5f9e5c11ac9&id=6a966cb3f7&e=5d8d80652b)
---
| | , **“Show me your papers” laws are anti-American.** Requiring voters to produce birth certificates, passports, and other documents to prove citizenship before they can register to vote is nothing more than a stunt designed to suppress the vote. Who does it hit the hardest? Working Texans. It especially burdens married women who have taken their spouse’s name and now have to track down documents that do not match. Many of these voters often do not have the time, the money, or the transportation needed to gather paperwork simply to exercise a fundamental American right. We never used to do this, and we’ve been around for 250 years. So, why now? **Because voter suppression is the point.** Add it all up. Thirty-day registration deadlines before voting, limits on voting by mail, closing countywide polling locations on Election Day, constantly shifting districts through mid-census gerrymandering. The list goes on. You can see exactly what the MAGA hyenas are doing to our precious right to vote. **I am running for Texas Attorney General to do the opposite.** I want Texans voting. I want Texans registered. I want Texans participating in the democracy that belongs to them. [**As Attorney General, I will use the law to defeat voter suppression wherever it appears. The Office of Attorney General should be a champion for participation, not a weapon against it.**](https://jaworskifortexas.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2e1f50319ad85f5f9e5c11ac9&id=ebb39da4c0&e=5d8d80652b) Texans deserve an elections advocate in that office. And when we do this right, voting in Texas will be easier, not harder. I am respectfully asking for your vote in the **May 26th, 2026 Democratic Primary runoff**. **Early voting runs May 18th through May 22nd.** [**Let’s defend the vote and strengthen our democracy together. Are you with me?**](https://jaworskifortexas.us17.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2e1f50319ad85f5f9e5c11ac9&id=623a7b41bd&e=5d8d80652b) Onward,

Students and young borrowers are too often dealing with a financial system that’s broken. Shady lenders and loan servicers are taking advantage of young people who are just trying to get an education.
In 2018, the Trump administration abruptly shuttered the Office for Students and Young Consumers, leaving millions of borrowers without any dedicated advocate or protection.
**That’s why I introduced the Students and Young Consumers Empowerment Act, which will reopen this critical office and ensure students have someone in their corner.**
The legislation will empower the office with new tools and a fresh mandate to demand industry data about risky loan practices, and it will give Congress better tools to hold the student loan industry accountable.
Our students deserve a fair shot at a quality and affordable education. I’ll always stand up for the next generation and fight to make our education system fairer — and I need you with me.

body:
New Hampshire’s Senate race is tied. And I’m rattled.

Folks, it’s James Carville.

I’ve worked on more campaigns than I can count, and let me tell you: **I don’t rattle easily.**

But this race in New Hampshire? **It’s TIED. In a dead heat. And that should scare the hell out of every Democrat in the country.**

[**_💥 Before you read another word, split a $10 donation between Chris Pappas and Maggie Hassan to help us pull ahead right now._**](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/127427728/608030375/1047731393?amount=10&refcode=LOC_EM_FR_2026.03.16_Pappas-Carville_B2_F1_S1_C1_90OP-NC_RS-T0&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDAvMS84ODg1OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjMmM3OTdiZC00NzIxLWYxMTEtOWE0OC0wMDBkM2ExNGI2NDAiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=e_8UVco6E5On9XLgAYSA0uog2RS6anr3bD_4bg1zKuY=) | | [ CHIP IN NOW >> ](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/127427729/608030376/1047731393?amount=10&refcode=LOC_EM_FR_2026.03.16_Pappas-Carville_B2_F1_S1_C1_90OP-NC_RS-T0&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQNDAvMS84ODg1OCIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJjMmM3OTdiZC00NzIxLWYxMTEtOWE0OC0wMDBkM2ExNGI2NDAiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=e_8UVco6E5On9XLgAYSA0uog2RS6anr3bD_4bg1zKuY=)
---
Here’s the deal: Jeanne Shaheen is retiring. That means this seat is wide open. **And now John Sununu — yes, one of those Sununus, the long-time New Hampshire political dynasty — is running to flip it red.**

He’s got the name, he’s got the money, and he’s got the full weight of the Republican donor class behind him — from Wall Street to the far-right Super PACs. They see New Hampshire as their ticket to locking down the Senate for another decade.

And right now? **This race is neck-and-neck. It could go either way.**

With St. Patrick's Day tomorrow, it's worth reflecting on Irish American Tom Brokaw's generation-defining book, _The Greatest Generation_. When it was published in 1998, it became an immediate, massive bestseller and coined a phrase that would lodge itself permanently in the American vocabulary -- a name for something Americans had never quite been able to articulate: the men and women who survived the Great Depression and then won the Second World War. Exceptional people defined by grit, stoicism, and moral clarity that subsequent generations simply haven't managed to replicate.
By the time Brokaw's book was published, those young soldiers were in their seventies. The women who had riveted aircraft and welded ships on the homefront were grandmothers. They had been home for half a century and spent their lives building families, communities, and the largest middle class growth in American history.

Most of them didn't talk about the war much. They certainly didn't think of themselves as heroes worthy of a moniker. They thought of themselves as lucky and kept working.
What made them capable of what they did wasn't some exceptional quality that skipped the generations that followed. Their success was a product of a system that made collective action possible at a scale we've never seen before or since. If we want another generation capable of that kind of resilience and grit, we must build institutions, opportunities, and collective resolve that allow ordinary people to rise in extraordinary moments.
The scale of what they lived through is easy to romanticize and just as easy to flatten. Sixteen million Americans served in uniform during World War II, roughly ten percent of the entire U.S. population at the time. The draft was mandatory, and more than 61 percent of those who served were conscripted. Casualties approached twelve percent.
A decade of Depression had already forced a kind of collective reckoning. Families who had lost everything understood shared sacrifice. The New Deal had rebuilt institutional trust and expanded the federal government's capacity to organize national life at scale. And the war itself, grim as it was, pulled the economy out of a stagnation that had lingered on for ten years, so that mobilization carried with it something that looks, in hindsight, almost like relief.
The United States redirected roughly 40 percent of its GDP to war production. American factories turned out 300,000 aircraft and 88,000 tanks. Civilian industries converted with astonishing speed. Female labor force participation rose from 27 to 37 percent, with six million women entering industrial jobs because the country needed them there. Public support for the war consistently exceeded 90 percent. Families bought war bonds, complied with rationing, and accepted constraints that would feel almost unthinkable today.
After the war, trust in the federal government hovered near 70 percent, and union membership reached about 35 percent of the workforce by the mid-1950s. Those numbers reflect something larger than policy preferences.
After the war, the GI Bill sent 7.8 million veterans to college or vocational training and backed 2.4 million home loans. Towns like Levittown in Bucks County, PA, and Long Island, NY, sprang up and created thriving suburbs. By 1947, veterans made up half of all college enrollments in the country. Half of the 16 million veterans started their own small businesses, creating iconic global brands like Walmart, Nike, and Comcast -- compared to just 5 percent of post-9/11 veterans today.
That generation also believed in public service. Seventy-eight percent of Congress was comprised of veterans, and three WWII veterans became president: Dwight Eisenhower, John F. Kennedy, and George H.W. Bush. Today, that number has fallen to 18 percent. It was a large-scale redeployment of human capital that generated decades of growth and social mobility -- the greatest expansion of the American middle class. The WWII generation made the tough choices for the betterment of the nation, going from 100% debt-to-GDP in 1946 down to 23% within thirty years. Now our generation is saddled once again with debt-to-GDP over 100% -- the product of an aging population, remilitarization, and a near-total absence of fiscal discipline with $38 trillion in debt.

The character of the generation mattered, but character alone doesn't build a middle class. Institutions and opportunities do.
Those institutions are exactly what's missing today. The clearest example is semiconductors. The United States currently manufactures roughly zero percent of the world's most advanced chips, nearly all of which come from a single facility in Taiwan. That's a structural dependency of the kind that 1940s American industrial policy would have treated as a national emergency. Semiconductor manufacturing is starting to come back to the U.S. thanks to private and public investment through the bipartisan CHIPS Act, but we're decades behind where we should be.
Active duty military today represents about 0.4 percent of the U.S. population. Trust in the federal government sits near 20 percent -- a record low that has held stubbornly for years. The information environment is fragmented to the point where shared factual reality is no longer something we can take for granted in policy debates. Geopolitical threats are real but diffuse: cyber warfare, economic weaponization, supply chain fragility, and adversaries who have studied our vulnerabilities for decades.
## **After Iraq & Afghanistan, we failed another defining test.**
We came home to a country that had barely noticed we were gone. No war bonds, no rationing, no shared sacrifice, just a volunteer force absorbing the weight of two decades of war while the rest of America went shopping. When COVID-19 arrived in early 2020, it briefly looked like the kind of unifying crisis that might force the broader reckoning we'd never had. In theory, it had all the ingredients that once produced broad civic mobilization: danger that did not discriminate and stakes that were unmistakable, with over one million Americans dying from Covid.
What happened instead was an almost perfect inversion of the 1940s model. The threat was contested almost from the beginning, refracted through a media ecosystem that had already sorted Americans into separate informational bubbles. Sacrifice fell almost entirely on essential workers, delivery drivers, and nurses while professional-class Americans retreated to home offices and rediscovered sourdough and banana bread (if you had teenagers, they were into making slime at the time). Some families even sprayed their mail with Lysol before opening it up. Public trust, which had been declining for years, deteriorated further in real time. Instead of converging around a shared understanding of the moment, the country fractured over whether the moment required collective action at all. No doubt some communities went too far, while some brazen political leaders didn't adhere to the same standards they implemented for their constituents.
The social infrastructure that made collective action possible in the 1940s has also been eroding for decades. Union membership has fallen from that postwar peak of 35 percent to around ten percent today. Church attendance, civic organizations, local newspapers, even bowling leagues -- the connective tissue of shared American life has thinned considerably. Remote work and algorithmic social media have accelerated a kind of atomization that makes the coordinated sacrifice of the war years feel not just distant but structurally impossible to replicate.
We've already seen this debate play out in one of the biggest bestsellers from last year.
Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson argue in their book _Abundance_ that America has lost the ability to do big things -- to build housing, infrastructure, and clean energy at scale -- because decades of well-intentioned regulation have prioritized process over outcomes. Their implicit model for what government capacity should look like is the 1940s, when the federal government could convert a civilian economy into a war machine in months.

What made the war effort possible was institutional readiness and the capacity to convert a civilian economy into a war machine in months because the government had spent a decade rebuilding its ability to act.
The next structural test is already taking shape. Advances in AI are already reshaping labor markets, concentrating economic power, and accelerating industrial transitions at a pace that could make previous disruptions seem gradual.
But we can build toward something better. The Greatest Generation didn't inherit good conditions. They inherited a Depression, a war, and a government that had spent a decade figuring out how to do things at scale. What they had, by the time the real test arrived, was institutional infrastructure capable of channeling individual effort into collective outcomes.
Building that infrastructure now -- for AI displacement, for the next pandemic, for the geopolitical pressures already accumulating -- is the actual work. It's less dramatic than storming a beach. It's also less optional than we're currently treating it.

Forty years from 9/11 in 2041, someone will be writing about our Post 9/11 generation, including many of us who served in America's longest wars in Iraq and Afghanistan. The only question is whether they'll describe a generation that met its moment in America's private and public sectors - or one that failed to face its challenges to create a better nation when called to.

> On Tuesday, February 24, 2026, President Trump delivered his much-anticipated State of the Union (SOTU) speech to both chambers of congress, and to the American people. Let's just say the evening was anything but a traditional address to the nation by its commander in chief. If you were one of the few that tuned in expecting a dignified Democrat party, one that conducts themselves with decorum and self-respect, you were sorely mistaken.
> [Upgrade to paid](https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9oZWFydGxhbmRqb3VybmFsLnN1YnN0YWNrLmNvbS9zdWJzY3JpYmU_.54w8XIvSvoFKOdANbBQQT1BHn5bzTnf-PRh5WZiMFk0?&utm_medium=email&utm_source=subscribe-widget&utm_content=191035367)
> As President Trump took to the podium to deliver his patriotic pitch to the American people, the Democrat attendees were quick to turn the stately event into a circus, showcasing once again how classless and unstable they've become. As if on cue, Representative Al Geen once again began to throw a juvenile tantrum, waving a sign and yelling slurs while POTUS calmy delivered his opening remarks. For the second year in a row, the buffoonish legislator from Texas was removed by Capitol Police within the first five minutes of the SOTU speech. Thanks to redistricting, his clown show will be concluding shortly.
>
> The complete lack of decorum didn't end with Representative Al Green's ejection, Representatives Ilhan Omar and Rashita Talib the so-called "squad members" painted a vivid picture of what the Democrat party has truly become. The two U.S. representatives attempted to turn the traditionally dignified evening into a circus, straight out of a middle school cafeteria food fight. Talib wearing a "FUCK ICE" pin on her lapel, while the two psychotic legislators began furiously screaming at the president during his remarks.
>
> Throughout the evening, Trump stood his ground, reminding all of us why he's in charge and not easily shaken or deterred. Despite unprecedented disruptions throughout the night, Trump remained resolute, highlighting his administrations achievements and reaffirming his commitments made to the American people. "Promises made, promises kept," "and into the golden age of America we go," he stated. But his words didn't just flow from the podium, they echoed throughout the chamber, resonating with supporters who cheered him on as if he were a rock star banging out their favorite tune.
>
> In one of many particularly emotional moments, he recognized a wounded National Guardsman who had been shot in the face while patrolling D.C., by an illegal Afghan alien. Trump then expanded his remarks to include several other families affected by violent crimes committed by illegal aliens and habitual violent offenders, promising these families justice. This prompted another standing ovation from many in the chamber; except for the feckless Democrats who sat on their hands but stood firmly in their soulless protections of criminal illegal aliens, and the carnage they continue to commit on innocent Americans.
>
> Also in attendance were the parents of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee who was savagely murdered, having her throat slit on a Charlotte North Carolina subway after working her shift that day by recidivist violent criminal offender. This was a heartbreaking moment of a woman who was able to escape war torn Ukraine, only to have her young life snuffed out by another Democrat run cashless bail city. Her parents were honored with a standing ovation by most in the gallery, except the Democrats, who once again continued to sit on their blood stained hands.
>
> The Democrat spectacle served as a glaring reminder of two very important things: First, they are simply incapable of civility in any setting, especially in the people's house; but probably more importantly, showed why they can never be trusted to lead the country in any capacity until they rid themselves of the radical fringe that has hijacked a once honorable political party. The party once thought of as the party of JFK, is now correctly dubbed the party of AOC.
>
> One thing is certain, the evening served as a microcosm of the state of affairs within the Democrat party. Trumps resilience amidst the fervent hostility exemplifies a fire brand of leadership that unapologetically refuses to back down, even in the face of adversity. It's a brand of leadership rarely seen in American politics and parallels the audaciousness of America's founding fathers.

Nothing says "State of the Union" like a speech, a spectacle, and a live audition for America's loudest reality show. | | | Mar 16 | | | | | | | | | | | | | | ---|---|--- On Tuesday, February 24, 2026, President Trump delivered his much-anticipated State of the Union (SOTU) speech to both chambers of congress, and to the American people. Let's just say the evening was anything but a traditional address to the nation by its commander in chief. If you were one of the few that tuned in expecting a dignified Democrat party, one that conducts themselves with decorum and self-respect, you were sorely mistaken. As President Trump took to the podium to deliver his patriotic pitch to the American people, the Democrat attendees were quick to turn the stately event into a circus, showcasing once again how classless and unstable they've become. As if on cue, Representative Al Geen once again began to throw a juvenile tantrum, waving a sign and yelling slurs while POTUS calmy delivered his opening remarks. For the second year in a row, the buffoonish legislator from Texas was removed by Capitol Police within the first five minutes of the SOTU speech. Thanks to redistricting, his clown show will be concluding shortly. The complete lack of decorum didn't end with Representative Al Green's ejection, Representatives Ilhan Omar and Rashita Talib the so-called "squad members" painted a vivid picture of what the Democrat party has truly become. The two U.S. representatives attempted to turn the traditionally dignified evening into a circus, straight out of a middle school cafeteria food fight. Talib wearing a "FUCK ICE" pin on her lapel, while the two psychotic legislators began furiously screaming at the president during his remarks. Throughout the evening, Trump stood his ground, reminding all of us why he's in charge and not easily shaken or deterred. Despite unprecedented disruptions throughout the night, Trump remained resolute, highlighting his administrations achievements and reaffirming his commitments made to the American people. "Promises made, promises kept," "and into the golden age of America we go," he stated. But his words didn't just flow from the podium, they echoed throughout the chamber, resonating with supporters who cheered him on as if he were a rock star banging out their favorite tune. In one of many particularly emotional moments, he recognized a wounded National Guardsman who had been shot in the face while patrolling D.C., by an illegal Afghan alien. Trump then expanded his remarks to include several other families affected by violent crimes committed by illegal aliens and habitual violent offenders, promising these families justice. This prompted another standing ovation from many in the chamber; except for the feckless Democrats who sat on their hands but stood firmly in their soulless protections of criminal illegal aliens, and the carnage they continue to commit on innocent Americans. Also in attendance were the parents of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee who was savagely murdered, having her throat slit on a Charlotte North Carolina subway after working her shift that day by recidivist violent criminal offender. This was a heartbreaking moment of a woman who was able to escape war torn Ukraine, only to have her young life snuffed out by another Democrat run cashless bail city. Her parents were honored with a standing ovation by most in the gallery, except the Democrats, who once again continued to sit on their blood stained hands. The Democrat spectacle served as a glaring reminder of two very important things: First, they are simply incapable of civility in any setting, especially in the people's house; but probably more importantly, showed why they can never be trusted to lead the country in any capacity until they rid themselves of the radical fringe that has hijacked a once honorable political party. The party once thought of as the party of JFK, is now correctly dubbed the party of AOC. One thing is certain, the evening served as a microcosm of the state of affairs within the Democrat party. Trumps resilience amidst the fervent hostility exemplifies a fire brand of leadership that unapologetically refuses to back down, even in the face of adversity. It's a brand of leadership rarely seen in American politics and parallels the audaciousness of America's founding fathers. # [](https://act.katieporter.com/go/21486?t=1&akid=40974%2E3422442%2E68qWBZ)
Peter, we talk a lot with you about the polls, about pushing for free child care, about less expensive housing, and about fighting for working Californians.
But today, I want to talk about the rest of me and what my life actually looks like.
When the cameras are off and the whiteboard is packed away, I’m just a single mom trying to keep up with the same everyday things a lot of families deal with.
I drive a minivan. I make dinner for my kids. And recently, I finally got ahead of a mountain of laundry that was waiting to be folded. The other night I even made a coconut white chocolate cake for my book club (recipe is **[here](https://act.katieporter.com/go/21722?t=3&akid=40974%2E3422442%2E68qWBZ)**!)
[](https://act.katieporter.com/go/21531?c0=em_ms_kp_20260316_1_ak.Vb_Zcx&refcode=em20260316-40974&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=4&akid=40974%2E3422442%2E68qWBZ)
Moments like this—driving the kids to activities, cooking dinner, catching up with friends—remind me why I’m running. Life shouldn't feel this hard for working families.
Too many Californians are juggling sky-high child care, full-time jobs, and rising housing costs. Too many politicians are completely disconnected from real life.
I’m running for governor because I know what it’s like to balance a budget at the kitchen table. I know how stressful it is when costs keep rising but paychecks don’t.
My campaign is powered by grassroots supporters who believe California should work for the people who live here, not billionaires, lobbyists, or corporations writing massive checks.
**[If you can, will you chip in $5 today to help us get our message out, reach as many voters as possible, and keep California in the hands of working families, not out-of-touch politicians?](https://act.katieporter.com/go/21531?c0=em_ms_kp_20260316_1_ak.Vb_Zcx&refcode=em20260316-40974&amounts=5%2C20%2C50%2C100%2C250%2C500%2C1000&t=5&akid=40974%2E3422442%2E68qWBZ)**

Thanks for being part of this,
Katie

| | March is here, and this month matters more than most. My FEC End-of-Quarter deadline isn’t just a date on a calendar. It’s one of the few opportunities we have to empower Democrats to **flip the Senate majority in 2026.** A Democratic majority means passing smart legislation, blocking extremist policies, and delivering _real_ results for communities across Maryland and the country. If you'd like to join my fight for families and freedom, [**please chip in $25 to help me hit my FEC goal so I can focus on what matters most.**](https://act.angelaalsobrooks.com/go/40418?t=9&amount=25&akid=3494%2E52803%2Ezkazl_) | | | [Chip in](https://act.angelaalsobrooks.com/go/40418?t=10&amount=25&akid=3494%2E52803%2Ezkazl_)

Even in the Senate minority, I’m working every day to push progress forward.
Just in the past few weeks, I’ve introduced legislation restoring federal loan access for graduate students, pushed for stronger protections for public health, and helped secure nearly **$30 million in federal funding for clean water and infrastructure projects across Maryland communities**.
I have also been out in the community and standing up for our values:
* I met with Lupita Nyong’o and advocates, researchers, and doctors focused on uterine fibroids to discuss expanding screening, detection, and intervention.
* I spoke at the National Network for Youth Congressional Briefing about my _Bipartisan Homeless Children and Youth Act_ , pushing for every young person to have a safe place to sleep at night.
* I visited the ICE facility in Baltimore for the second time to call out inhumane treatment.

These are real steps forward, Peter.
**But imagine how much further we could go with a Democratic Senate majority.**
Taking back the Senate majority will allow us to protect the progress we’ve made and deliver real results for families like yours.
I know you care about our communities as much as I do.
**That’s why I’m asking:[Will you chip in $25 today to make sure we meet this critical March milestone before the end of the month? It’s Kamala Harris.
As you read this, Virginians are headed to the polls to decide whether their voices will be heard in the midterms as they fight for fair elections.
Virginia’s redistricting ballot measure matters beyond just the Commonwealth. A **YES** vote on this amendment before Election Day on April 21 will ensure that **people, not politicians, have the final say.** If it doesn’t pass, Trump’s unprecedented power grabs across the country could keep his allies in power for years and significantly damage our democracy.
[**If that is all you need to hear to make a contribution, please donate now. I will explain more about why I am supporting this effort below.**](https://act.virginiansforfairelections.com/go/41?c0=em_ms_vafe_20260316_1.KV87kO&amount=3&refcode=20260316-338&t=2&akid=338%2E12592%2E4tOLr8)
Trump-aligned groups are already pouring millions of dollars into ads to convince Virginians to vote NO. They’re shifting from courtroom battles to spreading misinformation, trying to confuse voters before most people understand the stakes of this race.
**That’s why I am proud to join the fight alongside Virginians for Fair Elections.** Every day, they are working hard to educate voters, cut through mis- and disinformation, and make sure Virginia voters understand exactly what this amendment represents: preventing Trump’s power grabs across the nation and fighting back against Republicans’ attempt to rig the 2026 midterms.
I am asking you to act now because early voting has already started. [**Virginians for Fair Elections needs your help to reach voters across the Commonwealth before April 21. I’m pissed off because Republicans are in control of Washington, and what have they actually done for working people? Not a thing.

Instead, they’ve ripped away health care, cut life-saving programs like SNAP, and attacked Social Security benefits — the things we’ve all paid into and earned.

I’ve spent my life as a firefighter and union member. I know what it means to work hard, day in and day out, and I know what it feels like when Washington forgets about people like us. That’s why I’m running for Congress — to fight for working families, to stand up to billionaires, pass universal healthcare, and to make sure every voice in PA-07 is heard.

My opponent, Ryan Mackenzie? He’s spent his time in office voting in lockstep with Trump and his Republican bosses, voting to slash health care for people right here in this district — all to benefit his billionaire backers.

But if we organize, pitch in, and show the power of grassroots support, we can flip this seat and send a message that we are not going to sit by while Washington ignores us.

Friend, This may be hard for some to hear, but several years ago, I experienced a miscarriage. It was one of the most painful moments of my life. **To protect my own health, my doctor recommended a procedure, one that is medically charted as an abortion. ** I took comfort in knowing that they could do their jobs and provide the care I needed without fear of prosecution. **Today, women in Tennessee no longer have that assurance.** Doctors are forced to consult lawyers instead of focusing on patients, and women are left fearing whether lifesaving care will come in time,_if at all._ **Sadly, this reality is part of a broader crisis facing women all across Tennessee.** ******Tennessee has one of the highest maternal mortality rates in the country** —about 41 deaths for every 100,000 births, nearly twice the national average. Experts estimate that roughly **76% of pregnancy-related deaths are preventable. ** Making it worse, nearly half of Tennesseans live in childcare deserts, making it difficult for mothers to work and support their families. Women also continue to earn only about 83 cents for every dollar earned by men, and too many families, especially single mothers, are struggling to make ends meet. _**We cannot accept this as the status quo.**_ | | [FUEL OUR FIGHT FOR WOMEN](https://click.ngpvan.com/k/127434006/608048083/-843357993?refcode=3.16.26_WomenPlan&nvep=ew0KICAiVGVuYW50VXJpIjogIm5ncHZhbjovL3Zhbi9OR1AvTkdQMTAvMS83ODg3MyIsDQogICJEaXN0cmlidXRpb25VbmlxdWVJZCI6ICJkOTllYzAxZi00ZTIxLWYxMTEtOWE0OC0wMDBkM2ExNGI2NDAiLA0KICAiRW1haWxBZGRyZXNzIjogImRwd2lsbGlzNjdAZ21haWwuY29tIg0KfQ%3D%3D&hmac=rGfgniwCVSnw9b0kuFJlMHtePbPfFTfrRW6XH8ggvmE=)

We have a plan to bring women’s healthcare out of the stone age, and into the 21st century, and it begins with decisive action **STARTING DAY ONE:**
**DECLARE A MATERNAL HEALTH EMERGENCY**
Emergency grants to restore OB services at hospitals
**EXPAND POSTPARTUM MEDICAID COVERAGE**
12 months of coverage for eligible mothers
**PROTECT REPRODUCTIVE FREEDOM**
Executive order allowing doctors to practice without fear of prosecution
**CHILDCARE FOR ALL**
Use $50M in TANF funding to clear the childcare waitlist
**EXPAND ACCESS TO CONTRACEPTION**
Free contraception through the Department of Health
**PROTECT DOMESTIC VIOLENCE SURVIVORS**
Strengthen protective order enforcement statewide
**GUN SAFETY FOR FAMILIES**
Massively expand Tennessee’s free gun lock distribution program
**EQUAL PAY FOR WOMEN**
Equal pay certification for state contractors
We will also ensure that **no family is stuck on a waitlist for childcare** by launching a statewide childcare stabilization program ensuring parents can find care when they need it. And **we will invest in rural hospitals** to restore maternity services in communities that have lost them.
When women are _healthy, safe, and economically secure_ , families and communities can thrive. clean_body: | Friend, This may be hard for some to hear, but several years ago, I experienced a miscarriage. It was one of the most painful moments of my life. To protect my own health, my doctor recommended a procedure, one that is medically charted as an abortion. I took comfort in knowing that they could do their jobs and provide the care I needed without fear of prosecution. Today, women in Tennessee no longer have that assurance. Doctors are forced to consult lawyers instead of focusing on patients, and women are left fearing whether lifesaving care will come in time,if at all. Sadly, this reality is part of a broader crisis facing women all across Tennessee. ****Tennessee has one of the highest maternal mortality rates in the country —about 41 deaths for every 100,000 births, nearly twice the national average. Experts estimate that roughly 76% of pregnancy-related deaths are preventable. Making it worse, nearly half of Tennesseans live in childcare deserts, making it difficult for mothers to work and support their families. Women also continue to earn only about 83 cents for every dollar earned by men, and too many families, especially single mothers, are struggling to make ends meet. We cannot accept this as the status quo. | | = We have a plan to bring women’s healthcare out of the stone age, and into the 21st century, and it begins with decisive action STARTING DAY ONE: DECLARE A MATERNAL HEALTH EMERGENCY Emergency grants to restore OB services at hospitals EXPAND POSTPARTUM MEDICAID COVERAGE 12 months of coverage for eligible mothers PROTECT REPRODUCTIVE FREEDOM Executive order allowing doctors to practice without fear of prosecution CHILDCARE FOR ALL Use $50M in TANF funding to clear the childcare waitlist EXPAND ACCESS TO CONTRACEPTION Free contraception through the Department of Health PROTECT DOMESTIC VIOLENCE SURVIVORS Strengthen protective order enforcement statewide GUN SAFETY FOR FAMILIES Massively expand Tennessee’s free gun lock distribution program EQUAL PAY FOR WOMEN Equal pay certification for state contractors We will also ensure that no family is stuck on a waitlist for childcare by launching a statewide childcare stabilization program ensuring parents can find care when they need it. And we will invest in rural hospitals to restore maternity services in communities that have lost them. When women are healthy, safe, and economically secure , families and communities can thrive. = If you've saved your payment information with ActBlue Express, your donation will go through immediately: | = = | = = | = = Together, we will build a Tennessee where every woman has the care, opportunity, and dignity she deserves. We need to raise $100,000 by MIDNIGHT tonight to power our intense voter mobilization all over this state. In a race as close and expensive as this, we can’t afford to fall short in the final hours.
